screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will meet Blueprints, Unreal Engine’s visual scripting system that lets you build gameplay without writing C++ lines. Blueprints represent logic as nodes you connect; each node is an event, an action, or data. You’ll create a new Blueprint Class derived from Actor, open the Blueprint Editor, identify the Components, My Blueprint, Details, and Event Graph panels, and then wire an Event BeginPlay to a Print String node so you see text when the game starts. This workflow — pick a parent class, add components, connect nodes, compile, and save — is the core loop you will repeat with increasing complexity. As you follow along, notice how events trigger execution pins, and how data pins pass values like text or object references. A common beginner mistake is forgetting to compile after edits; compiling verifies and converts the visual graph into executable code. By the end you’ll drag your new Blueprint into the level and press Play to confirm the result. Think about what small feedback you want first: a debug message, a sound, or a visibility toggle. That choice guides which nodes you attach next.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Your First Blueprint
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Your First Blueprint

Create a simple Actor Blueprint, wire Event BeginPlay to a Print String, compile, save, and test in-play.

16:9 HD Classroom

Blueprints let designers and artists implement gameplay by assembling nodes instead of typing code. Each node either responds to an event or performs an action; connecting execution pins builds the sequence that runs at runtime.

This lesson shows the exact beginner workflow and highlights common mistakes, like forgetting to compile, and good practice, such as naming your Blueprint clearly.

Explore Key Topics
Create Blueprint Class
Pick Actor as parent and name BP_MyFirstInteractiveObject.
Event Graph & Nodes
Use events like BeginPlay and action nodes such as Print String.
Compile & Test
Compile converts the graph into executable code; Save preserves the asset.
Visual Idea
Blueprint Class
Event & Action
Compile & Save
Think of Blueprints as wiring a short circuit: events supply the electricity, action nodes use it, and compilation locks the connections into executable form.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives set a clear path for your first Blueprint. You will understand what Blueprint visual scripting is, and why it is a practical alternative for designers who prefer node-based logic over text-based programming. You will create a Blueprint Class derived from Actor so the asset can be placed and tested in a level. You will confidently navigate the Blueprint Editor panels — Components, My Blueprint, Event Graph, and Details — and know where to find variables, functions, and events. You will identify and add basic nodes such as Event BeginPlay and Print String, and connect execution and data pins to form a working script. Finally, you will compile and save the Blueprint, understanding that compile validates and converts your graph into executable code and that save persists the asset. Each objective includes a small practice: creating BP_MyFirstInteractiveObject, wiring Event BeginPlay to a Print String, and placing the Blueprint in the level to verify the message appears during Play. Keep an eye out for the common mistake of skipping compilation; it’s the most likely cause of changes not appearing in-game.

screens.title: What is a Blueprint?
screens.narratorSegment: A Blueprint is Unreal Engine’s node-based visual scripting system that represents game logic as connected blocks instead of lines of text. Think of each node as a single responsibility: one node can be an Event that triggers when the game starts, another can be an Action that prints text, and others pass data like numbers or object references. This structure is powerful because it separates control flow from implementation details and makes logic visible and discoverable. For example, to run a message at startup you use Event BeginPlay as the trigger and a Print String action to show text. Because Blueprints compile into native code, performance is suitable for many gameplay systems, and artists or designers can iterate without deep C++ knowledge. A common misconception is that Blueprints are only for prototypes; in reality they are used throughout many shipped games. However, complex systems may still use C++ for low-level or highly optimized code. The practical takeaway is that Blueprints let you implement interactive behavior quickly, verify changes by compiling, and then test the result in Play. Consider how the node metaphor maps to small, testable responsibilities in your designs.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › What is a Blueprint?
Definition

Blueprints are node-based assets that package components, variables, and event graphs into a reusable class. They can be placed in a level or instantiated at runtime.

Event: Event BeginPlay — fires once when the Actor spawns or the game starts.
Action: Print String — displays a text message on screen for debugging or feedback.
Data pins — carry values like text, numbers, or object references between nodes.
Key Takeaway

Blueprints expose logic visually and compile to executable code for safe, fast iteration.

Analogy

Imagine wiring small appliances: an event supplies power, action nodes are devices that perform a task, and data pins are the cords carrying values. The graph shows the wiring at a glance.

Common Misconception

Blueprints are not only for prototypes. They can be production-grade, but very low-level systems sometimes remain in C++ for optimization.

Example
Event BeginPlay → Print String("Hello from my first Blueprint!")

screens.title: Create a Blueprint Class
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a Blueprint Class is the first practical step to add interactive objects to your level. Start in the Content Browser: right-click, choose Blueprint Class, and you’ll see a Pick Parent Class dialog. The parent class determines what your new Blueprint can do by default. For a simple interactive prop, pick Actor. If you need movement and player control, pick Character. After choosing Actor, give your asset a descriptive name like BP_MyFirstInteractiveObject or BP_WelcomeMessage. This naming helps you find the asset later and keeps the project organized. Open the new Blueprint by double-clicking the asset; the Blueprint Editor loads with default panels and often with three default events in the Event Graph. A common beginner mistake is selecting the wrong parent and later discovering missing features; it’s quicker to pick the closest parent and refactor if necessary than to struggle with mismatched behavior. Finally, add a StaticMeshComponent if your object needs a visible form. Assign a mesh such as SM_Cylinder from StarterContent and scale it appropriately. These steps produce a placeable Blueprint Class ready for logic and testing. Create a Blueprint Class means choose an appropriate parent (actor for props), name the blueprint clearly, add components, and open the event graph to start wiring logic.. In practical terms, step-by-step: content browser → pick parent → name. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Create a Blueprint Class
Step-by-step
  1. In Content Browser, right-click → Blueprint Class.
  2. In Pick Parent Class, select Actor for props.
  3. Name asset like BP_MyFirstInteractiveObject.
  4. Double-click to open the Blueprint Editor.
Add a Component
Click Add > StaticMeshComponent, then assign SM_Cylinder and set scale to 0.5, 0.5, 0.5 if using StarterContent.
Key Takeaway

Choose the right parent class and give meaningful names to make iteration and collaboration faster.

Concrete Example
BP_WelcomeMessage: Actor parent, StaticMeshComponent with SM_Cylinder, event logic added in the Event Graph.
Common Mistake

Picking Character when you just need a prop adds unnecessary components and may confuse movement or collision expectations.

screens.title: Blueprint Editor Panels
screens.narratorSegment: The Blueprint Editor groups the pieces you need to assemble an asset. The Components panel lists every Component attached to the Blueprint — for example a StaticMeshComponent gives your Blueprint a visible form. Below that, the My Blueprint panel lists variables, functions, macros, and event graphs; use it to add a variable that stores state or a function to encapsulate reusable logic. The Details panel shows properties for any selected component or node; use Details to set mesh, transform, or default values for variables. The Event Graph is the central canvas where you add Events and Action nodes and wire execution and data pins. A typical layout places Components and My Blueprint on the left, Event Graph in the center, and Details on the right. Knowing where to find and edit each element is crucial for efficient work: add components to the left, inspect properties on the right, and build the behavior in the center. A misconception is that only the Event Graph matters — in truth, components and variables are equally important because they represent the Blueprint’s state and structure used by the graph.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Blueprint Editor Panels
Components
Lists the Blueprint’s Components. Add StaticMeshComponent, Collision, or Audio components here. Drag a component into the graph to get a reference.
My Blueprint
Contains variables, functions, and event graphs. Use variables to store state like a boolean toggle for visibility.
Details
Shows editable properties of the selected object. Set default values, change meshes, or adjust collision settings here.
Event Graph (center canvas)
Events: triggers like Event BeginPlay, Tick, or ActorBeginOverlap.
Actions: Print String, Toggle Visibility, Set Location.
Pins: white execution pins, colored data pins passing values.

screens.title: Event Graph: Events and Default Nodes
screens.narratorSegment: When you first open the Event Graph you’ll often see default events: Event BeginPlay, Event Tick, and Event ActorBeginOverlap. Event BeginPlay fires once when the Actor enters the level or the game starts — use it for initialization like printing a welcome message or setting initial properties. Event Tick fires every frame and is suitable for continuous updates such as smooth movement or real-time checks; avoid overusing Tick for simple one-off tasks because it runs constantly. Event ActorBeginOverlap fires when another Actor enters this Actor’s collision volume and is ideal for triggers, pickups, or toggles. To add an event manually, right-click in the graph and type the event name. The event sends an execution signal via a white execution pin to the next connected node. Data pins (colored) carry parameters: for example, ActorBeginOverlap provides a reference to the Other Actor. A common mistake is wiring heavy logic to Event Tick that should instead run only when required; this causes unnecessary C P U use. Practice adding Event BeginPlay, wiring Print String, and then consider whether your logic truly needs per-frame updates or event-driven triggers instead.

keyIdea.title: Events
keyIdea.text: Default events are entry points: BeginPlay for initialization, Tick for per-frame updates, and ActorBeginOverlap for collisions and triggers.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Event Graph: Events
Default Events
  • Event BeginPlay — runs once at start, ideal for setup.
  • Event Tick — runs each frame, use sparingly for continuous updates.
  • Event ActorBeginOverlap — runs when something overlaps this Actor’s collision.
Misconception

Tick is not a substitute for event-driven logic. Many behaviors are efficient when driven by overlap or custom events instead of per-frame checks.

Visual Walkthrough (pseudo graph)
Event BeginPlay -> Print String("Welcome to the game!") Event ActorBeginOverlap -> Toggle Visibility(StaticMeshComponent) Event Tick -> (optional) UpdatePosition(DeltaTime)
Tip: Inspect the pins — execution pins are white and control flow, data pins carry parameters like strings or actor references.

screens.title: Connect Execution and Data Pins
screens.narratorSegment: Connecting nodes is the act of defining flow and data in Blueprints. Execution pins are white and shape the order in which nodes run. Data pins are colored and carry values like text, numbers, booleans, and object references. To form a working script, drag from an execution pin to another node’s execution input; this creates a white wire. To pass a value, drag from a data pin to a compatible data input, for example a String data pin into a Print String node’s In String input. Type mismatches will show as incompatible; this safeguards correctness. Another common pattern is dragging a component from the Components panel into the graph to get a reference node whose colored pin you can connect as the Target for actions like Toggle Visibility. Avoid leaving execution wires disconnected — nodes with an execution output but no target will never run. Also avoid connecting heavy operations to loops or Tick without guards. Practically, think in small steps: trigger, action, optional data path. Always compile frequently to catch type errors and ensure the graph’s wiring is valid.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Connect Execution and Data Pins
Execution vs Data
Execution pins (white) form the order; data pins (colored) pass values. Connect execution to execution, and match data pin types when wiring values.
Example: Event BeginPlay → Print String
Example: Drag StaticMeshComponent into graph → connect its reference to Toggle Visibility Target.
Checklist for wiring
  • Ensure execution wires end at a node that performs work.
  • Confirm data pin types match expected input types.
  • Provide explicit targets to avoid ambiguous references.
  • Compile to surface type or connection errors early.
Pro-tip: Pull component references into the graph rather than relying on implicit defaults — explicit targets reduce bugs.

screens.title: Print String Example: Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: A Print String node is an ideal first action because it provides visible feedback in Play. To add it, locate Event BeginPlay in your Event Graph or right-click and add it if missing. Drag from Event BeginPlay’s white execution pin and type Print String in the context menu, selecting the node. The Print String node has an In String input where you type your message, and a Duration property that sets how long it stays on screen. For debugging, set a short duration such as 2 seconds; for a welcome message set it longer, like 5 seconds. After wiring and setting the message, click Compile. If the Compile indicator turns green, there are no critical errors; then click Save to persist the Blueprint asset. Finally, drag an instance of the Blueprint into your level and press Play to see the message appear in the top-left. If you don’t see the message, verify that the Blueprint instance is present in the level and that you compiled the asset. Common beginner mistakes include forgetting to compile and leaving the message blank. The Print String workflow teaches the full create-wire-test loop in a compact example.

keyIdea.title: Print String usage
keyIdea.text: Use Print String to provide quick on-screen feedback; set text and duration, then compile and test by placing the Blueprint in the level.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Print String Walkthrough
Quick steps
  1. Find or add Event BeginPlay in Event Graph.
  2. Drag from the white execution pin and add Print String.
  3. Enter message: "Welcome to the game!" and set Duration to 5.0.
  4. Compile, then Save, place the Blueprint, and Play.
Debug tip: use Print String to confirm that a path executes, then replace with game feedback like sound or animation.
Pseudo-code representation
Event BeginPlay -> Print String(In String: "Hello from my first Blueprint!", Duration: 5.0)
If you see no output, check that the Blueprint instance is present in the level and that you compiled the Blueprint after editing.

screens.title: Implement a Simple Toggle: BeginOverlap → Toggle Visibility
screens.narratorSegment: A small interactive challenge is adding a StaticMeshComponent and toggling its visibility when the player overlaps the Blueprint. First add a StaticMeshComponent in the Components panel and assign a mesh such as SM_Cylinder. Scale it to fit the scene. Next, in the Event Graph add Event ActorBeginOverlap by right-clicking and searching for it. Drag the StaticMeshComponent from the Components panel into the graph — this creates a reference node whose output pin you will use as the Target. From Event ActorBeginOverlap’s execution pin, add a Toggle Visibility node. Connect the execution flow and hook the StaticMeshComponent reference into the Toggle Visibility Target input. Toggle Visibility flips the visible state of the mesh each time an overlap occurs. Compile and Save your Blueprint, then place it in the level. When you play and move into the collision volume, you should see the mesh toggle between visible and hidden. Common mistakes include forgetting to connect the Target pin or expecting Toggle Visibility to automatically know which component to operate on; explicitly providing the component reference avoids ambiguity and is a robust practice.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Simple Toggle
Steps
  1. Add StaticMeshComponent and assign SM_Cylinder.
  2. Add Event ActorBeginOverlap in Event Graph.
  3. Drag StaticMeshComponent into graph and connect to Toggle Visibility Target.

screens.title: Compare Events: BeginPlay, Tick, ActorBeginOverlap
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right event is critical for correct and efficient behavior. Event BeginPlay runs once when the Actor becomes active; use it for initialization such as showing a welcome message or setting starting variables. Event Tick runs every frame and is suitable for smooth movement, timers, or continuous checks; however, Tick consumes C P U if overused. If your functionality is triggered by interaction, choose Event ActorBeginOverlap to respond only when another Actor enters your collision area — this is ideal for pickups, triggers, or toggles. As an example, use BeginPlay to print an initial message, ActorBeginOverlap to toggle visibility when players walk over a pickup area, and Tick only for continuous tasks like interpolating a door’s rotation. A frequent beginner error is hooking heavy logic to Tick that should be event-driven; this becomes expensive as the number of Actors grows. Another error is assuming BeginPlay will run later; BeginPlay runs when the Actor is started, which may be when the level loads or the Actor is spawned. Ask yourself: is this a one-time setup, an ongoing per-frame task, or an interaction-driven response? That question determines the correct event.

Event BeginPlay

Runs once at Actor start. Use for setup like Print String("Welcome to the game!") or initializing variables.

Runs each frame. Use for continuous updates but avoid heavy per-frame work to prevent performance issues.

screens.title: Compile and Save: Why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: Compiling is the step that checks your Blueprint graph for errors and converts the visual nodes into executable code the engine can use at runtime. Hitting Compile runs validation: it detects type mismatches, broken references, or disconnected execution nodes that will not run. A green Compile indicator means the Blueprint is syntactically valid and ready for testing. Saving persists the asset file in the Content Browser. Many beginners edit their graph but forget to compile, then wonder why changes do not appear when playing — compiling is required so the engine picks up the new logic. If you see warnings after compiling, inspect the message log and address them before playtesting. Another common error is modifying a Blueprint used in the level but not saving the map; while Blueprint assets save separately, keeping both asset and level saved reduces confusion. In practice, compile early and often after changes, then save. This keeps iteration fast and avoids chasing stale behavior during tests. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Compile and Save
Why Compile?
  • Validates connections and types.
  • Converts the graph into executable code for runtime.
  • Surfaces warnings and errors in the message log.
Common Errors & Fixes
Forgot to Compile — changes won't run until compiled.
Type mismatch — connect compatible data pin types or convert values explicitly.
Broken references — reassign components or variables if the asset was renamed or moved.
Procedure: edit graph → Compile (confirm green) → Save asset → Place in level → Play.

screens.title: Place and Test Your Blueprint
screens.narratorSegment: After creating and compiling your Blueprint, the final step is to place it in the level and verify behavior in Play. Open the Content Browser, find BP_MyFirstInteractiveObject or BP_WelcomeMessage, then drag an instance into the level viewport. For the Print String example, press Play — you should see the message appear in the top-left corner for the specified duration. For the overlap toggle, move the player into the Actor’s collision volume and observe the StaticMeshComponent toggling visibility. If behavior does not match expectations, retrace your steps: is the Blueprint instance actually in the level? Did you compile the Blueprint after making changes? Are execution wires connected? Are you using the right event for the intended behavior? Testing iteratively helps isolate problems quickly: change a single node, compile, save, and retest. Keep the test focused — one change per run — so you can identify the cause of unexpected behavior. This disciplined approach speeds learning and reduces frustration as you scale up from simple messages to more complex gameplay systems. Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Place and Test
Testing checklist
  • Drag the Blueprint into the level from the Content Browser.
  • Ensure the instance is positioned where the player can see or interact with it.

If behavior appears, proceed to add small enhancements like sound or animation.
If behavior fails, check compile status, connections, and that the instance exists in the level.

Testing is part of the authoring loop: build small, test often, and keep changes incremental for faster troubleshooting.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will meet Blueprints, Unreal Engine’s visual scripting system that lets you build gameplay without writing C++ lines. Blueprints represent logic as nodes you connect; each node is an event, an action, or data. You’ll create a new Blueprint Class derived from Actor, open the Blueprint Editor, identify the Components, My Blueprint, Details, and Event Graph panels, and then wire an Event BeginPlay to a Print String node so you see text when the game starts. This workflow — pick a parent class, add components, connect nodes, compile, and save — is the core loop you will repeat with increasing complexity. As you follow along, notice how events trigger execution pins, and how data pins pass values like text or object references. A common beginner mistake is forgetting to compile after edits; compiling verifies and converts the visual graph into executable code. By the end you’ll drag your new Blueprint into the level and press Play to confirm the result. Think about what small feedback you want first: a debug message, a sound, or a visibility toggle. That choice guides which nodes you attach next.

These objectives set a clear path for your first Blueprint. You will understand what Blueprint visual scripting is, and why it is a practical alternative for designers who prefer node-based logic over text-based programming. You will create a Blueprint Class derived from Actor so the asset can be placed and tested in a level. You will confidently navigate the Blueprint Editor panels — Components, My Blueprint, Event Graph, and Details — and know where to find variables, functions, and events. You will identify and add basic nodes such as Event BeginPlay and Print String, and connect execution and data pins to form a working script. Finally, you will compile and save the Blueprint, understanding that compile validates and converts your graph into executable code and that save persists the asset. Each objective includes a small practice: creating BP_MyFirstInteractiveObject, wiring Event BeginPlay to a Print String, and placing the Blueprint in the level to verify the message appears during Play. Keep an eye out for the common mistake of skipping compilation; it’s the most likely cause of changes not appearing in-game.

In this second objectives slide we'll connect learning outcomes to short verification tasks you can perform now. First, to show you understand Blueprint visual scripting, create BP_MyFirstInteractiveObject and explain in a sentence what nodes represent and how execution flow works. Second, to prove you can make a Blueprint Class, add a StaticMeshComponent, assign a mesh, and scale it — then describe why Actor was the correct parent. Third, to demonstrate navigation skills, point to the Event Graph and locate Event BeginPlay, My Blueprint, and Details; name one property you might edit in Details. Fourth, to confirm you can wire nodes and save, wire Event BeginPlay to a Print String with a custom message, compile until the compile button turns green, save the asset, and then place the Blueprint in a level and Play to see the message. Each task is short, repeatable, and focused. A misconception to watch for is assuming Save alone applies changes; compiling is the step that ensures the graph is valid and executable. These checks keep your development fast and repeatable.

A Blueprint is Unreal Engine’s node-based visual scripting system that represents game logic as connected blocks instead of lines of text. Think of each node as a single responsibility: one node can be an Event that triggers when the game starts, another can be an Action that prints text, and others pass data like numbers or object references. This structure is powerful because it separates control flow from implementation details and makes logic visible and discoverable. For example, to run a message at startup you use Event BeginPlay as the trigger and a Print String action to show text. Because Blueprints compile into native code, performance is suitable for many gameplay systems, and artists or designers can iterate without deep C++ knowledge. A common misconception is that Blueprints are only for prototypes; in reality they are used throughout many shipped games. However, complex systems may still use C++ for low-level or highly optimized code. The practical takeaway is that Blueprints let you implement interactive behavior quickly, verify changes by compiling, and then test the result in Play. Consider how the node metaphor maps to small, testable responsibilities in your designs.

Creating a Blueprint Class is the first practical step to add interactive objects to your level. Start in the Content Browser: right-click, choose Blueprint Class, and you’ll see a Pick Parent Class dialog. The parent class determines what your new Blueprint can do by default. For a simple interactive prop, pick Actor. If you need movement and player control, pick Character. After choosing Actor, give your asset a descriptive name like BP_MyFirstInteractiveObject or BP_WelcomeMessage. This naming helps you find the asset later and keeps the project organized. Open the new Blueprint by double-clicking the asset; the Blueprint Editor loads with default panels and often with three default events in the Event Graph. A common beginner mistake is selecting the wrong parent and later discovering missing features; it’s quicker to pick the closest parent and refactor if necessary than to struggle with mismatched behavior. Finally, add a StaticMeshComponent if your object needs a visible form. Assign a mesh such as SM_Cylinder from StarterContent and scale it appropriately. These steps produce a placeable Blueprint Class ready for logic and testing. Create a Blueprint Class means choose an appropriate parent (actor for props), name the blueprint clearly, add components, and open the event graph to start wiring logic.. In practical terms, step-by-step: content browser → pick parent → name. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Blueprint Editor groups the pieces you need to assemble an asset. The Components panel lists every Component attached to the Blueprint — for example a StaticMeshComponent gives your Blueprint a visible form. Below that, the My Blueprint panel lists variables, functions, macros, and event graphs; use it to add a variable that stores state or a function to encapsulate reusable logic. The Details panel shows properties for any selected component or node; use Details to set mesh, transform, or default values for variables. The Event Graph is the central canvas where you add Events and Action nodes and wire execution and data pins. A typical layout places Components and My Blueprint on the left, Event Graph in the center, and Details on the right. Knowing where to find and edit each element is crucial for efficient work: add components to the left, inspect properties on the right, and build the behavior in the center. A misconception is that only the Event Graph matters — in truth, components and variables are equally important because they represent the Blueprint’s state and structure used by the graph.

When you first open the Event Graph you’ll often see default events: Event BeginPlay, Event Tick, and Event ActorBeginOverlap. Event BeginPlay fires once when the Actor enters the level or the game starts — use it for initialization like printing a welcome message or setting initial properties. Event Tick fires every frame and is suitable for continuous updates such as smooth movement or real-time checks; avoid overusing Tick for simple one-off tasks because it runs constantly. Event ActorBeginOverlap fires when another Actor enters this Actor’s collision volume and is ideal for triggers, pickups, or toggles. To add an event manually, right-click in the graph and type the event name. The event sends an execution signal via a white execution pin to the next connected node. Data pins (colored) carry parameters: for example, ActorBeginOverlap provides a reference to the Other Actor. A common mistake is wiring heavy logic to Event Tick that should instead run only when required; this causes unnecessary C P U use. Practice adding Event BeginPlay, wiring Print String, and then consider whether your logic truly needs per-frame updates or event-driven triggers instead.

Connecting nodes is the act of defining flow and data in Blueprints. Execution pins are white and shape the order in which nodes run. Data pins are colored and carry values like text, numbers, booleans, and object references. To form a working script, drag from an execution pin to another node’s execution input; this creates a white wire. To pass a value, drag from a data pin to a compatible data input, for example a String data pin into a Print String node’s In String input. Type mismatches will show as incompatible; this safeguards correctness. Another common pattern is dragging a component from the Components panel into the graph to get a reference node whose colored pin you can connect as the Target for actions like Toggle Visibility. Avoid leaving execution wires disconnected — nodes with an execution output but no target will never run. Also avoid connecting heavy operations to loops or Tick without guards. Practically, think in small steps: trigger, action, optional data path. Always compile frequently to catch type errors and ensure the graph’s wiring is valid.

A Print String node is an ideal first action because it provides visible feedback in Play. To add it, locate Event BeginPlay in your Event Graph or right-click and add it if missing. Drag from Event BeginPlay’s white execution pin and type Print String in the context menu, selecting the node. The Print String node has an In String input where you type your message, and a Duration property that sets how long it stays on screen. For debugging, set a short duration such as 2 seconds; for a welcome message set it longer, like 5 seconds. After wiring and setting the message, click Compile. If the Compile indicator turns green, there are no critical errors; then click Save to persist the Blueprint asset. Finally, drag an instance of the Blueprint into your level and press Play to see the message appear in the top-left. If you don’t see the message, verify that the Blueprint instance is present in the level and that you compiled the asset. Common beginner mistakes include forgetting to compile and leaving the message blank. The Print String workflow teaches the full create-wire-test loop in a compact example.

A small interactive challenge is adding a StaticMeshComponent and toggling its visibility when the player overlaps the Blueprint. First add a StaticMeshComponent in the Components panel and assign a mesh such as SM_Cylinder. Scale it to fit the scene.
